issue: “A light woman” reads in English as “a woman of easy virtue”, a sense the Russian does not have; «легкая» here describes her light, dancing step.
old: he was overtaken by a light woman walking
new: he was overtaken by a light-footed woman walking

issue: «покрывало» is the same word as Niza’s black veil a few lines earlier; “cloth” loses the image of the heart fluttering like a bird under her veil.
old: like a bird under a black cloth
new: like a bird under a black veil

issue: Wrong detail: Judas is stabbed under the shoulder blade and through the heart (26:62); nobody cuts his throat. «зарезать» means to kill with a knife. This is the narrator stating fact, so it contradicts the scene. (See the systematic note in revEN-D.md on the other «зарезать» renderings in dialogue.)
old: Where the two who had cut Judas’s throat went
new: Where the two who had knifed Judas went

issue: «столбы с перекладинами» are posts that carry crossbeams (the crosses). “posts and crossbeams” reads as two separate things.
old: with emptied posts and crossbeams
new: with emptied posts bearing crossbeams

issue: English grammar: “out of Moscow to God knows how many kilometers away” combines two constructions.
russian: выбросить этого же Степу вон из Москвы за бог знает какое количество километров
old: throw that same Styopa out of Moscow to God knows how many kilometers away
new: throw that same Styopa out of Moscow, God knows how many kilometers away

issue: «в беспамятстве» here means in a daze or beside himself, not unconscious. An unconscious man cannot leave for Leningrad.
russian: в беспамятстве он уехал в Ленинград
old: in a state of unconsciousness had left for Leningrad
new: in a daze had left for Leningrad

issue: Negation inverted. «таких вещей, что не пришлось бы вам покинуть ваш пост» means “such things that you may well have to leave your post” (a threat). The English says the opposite: “that you might not have to leave”.
russian: что не пришлось бы вам покинуть ваш пост
old: that you might not have to leave your post
new: that you may well have to leave your post

issue: Stiff calque. «Все кусается» is the colloquial “everything’s so expensive”. “Everything bites” makes no sense in English.
old: “Everything bites,”
new: “Prices bite these days,”

issue: «порыжевший ботинок» is a shoe faded to a rusty brown with wear. “reddened” suggests it has turned red.
old: next to his reddened boot
new: next to his rusty, faded boot

issue: Calque. «Ты с чем пожаловал» is “what brings you here”. “What have you come with” makes the reader think he is carrying something.
old: What have you come with, uninvited but foreseen guest?
new: What brings you here, uninvited but foreseen guest?

issue: Echo of the darkness motif (19:21, 25:1; GLOSSARY): harmonisation changed 25:1 “that had come” to “that came”. «Эта тьма, пришедшая с запада» repeats the pattern, so the wording should match.
old: This darkness, which had come from the west
new: This darkness, which came from the west

issue: Echo of 25:1 «Тьма, пришедшая со Средиземного моря», where the GLOSSARY form is “The darkness that came from the Mediterranean Sea”. Margarita is quoting the chapter she has just read, so the wording should be identical.
russian: про тьму, которая пришла со Средиземного моря
old: the darkness that came in from the Mediterranean Sea
new: the darkness that came from the Mediterranean Sea

issue: Consistency: Azazello’s «бельмо» is “a film over one eye” (10:132) and “a white film over his left eye” (18:57). “Cataract” is a different condition.
old: the eye with the cataract
new: the eye with the white film

issue: Ambiguity that inverts the sense: «демон-убийца» is a murdering demon, but in English “demon-killer” reads as someone who kills demons.
old: the demon-killer
new: the killer demon

issue: Deliberate echo of Pilate’s words in 26:79, «У вас тоже плохая должность», rendered there as “Yours is a bad office too”. The same «плохая должность» should not become “post” here.
old: and that he has a bad post
new: and that he has a bad office

issue: Consistency: «трамвай» is “tram” throughout the book (1, 3, 4, 8, 18, 27, 31). Only the Epilogue switches to “streetcar”.
old: in streetcars
new: in trams

issue: Stiff word order: “the chemistry Candidate of Sciences Vetchinkevich” makes the reader stumble.
old: the chemistry Candidate of Sciences Vetchinkevich
new: Vetchinkevich, a Candidate of Chemical Sciences

issue: Consistency: «трамвай» is “tram” everywhere else (27:40, 27:51 for the same event).
old: drove Berlioz under the streetcar
new: drove Berlioz under the tram

issue: Wrong referent and a glossary break. The aunt herself is Porokhovnikova (15:107: «У тетки моей, Пороховниковой», “At my aunt’s, Porokhovnikova’s”; GLOSSARY “Porokhovnikova”). «Пороховниковой тетки» means “the aunt Porokhovnikova”. The English invents a “Porokhovnikov” whose aunt she is.
old: nor Porokhovnikov’s old skinflint of an aunt
new: nor that old skinflint of an aunt, Porokhovnikova

issue: Motif form: GLOSSARY renders «О боги» as “O gods” (2:3, 2:178, 24:166). “Oh gods” breaks the pattern.
old: Oh gods, how he lies!
new: O gods, how he lies!
